name: contacts
title: A contact book
pitch: Names, phone numbers, emails, saved in a file and searchable. In C, this small program teaches the big ideas: structs, memory you ask for and give back, linked lists, and checking your memory with valgrind.

steps.do: Write a struct contact with a name, a phone number and an email; fill one in your code and print it.
steps.hint: Fixed-size char arrays (`char name[64];`) and `strcpy` or `snprintf` to fill them.
steps.why: A struct is the shape of your data. Deciding the sizes now (64 characters for a name?) is a real design choice.

steps.do: Make an array of 3 contacts and print them all with a loop.
steps.hint: A function `print_contact(const struct contact *c)` keeps the loop short.
steps.why: Passing a pointer instead of the whole struct avoids copying it, and `const` promises the function won't change it.

steps.do: Read a contact typed by the user with fgets. Find out why `scanf("%s")` is dangerous here.
steps.done: a name with a space, like "Ada Lovelace", is read whole.
steps.hint: `fgets(buf, sizeof buf, stdin)`, then remove the `\n` at the end (`strcspn` finds it).
steps.why: `scanf("%s")` stops at the first space and doesn't know the size of your array: a long name writes past its end. That's a buffer overflow, one of the most common security holes in C.

steps.do: Create one contact with malloc, use it, and free it.
steps.done: the program prints it and frees it.
steps.hint: `malloc(sizeof *c)`, check it isn't NULL, `free(c)` when done.
steps.why: Memory from malloc lives on the heap until you free it: it outlives the function that made it. That freedom is why you must give it back yourself.

steps.do: Replace the array with a linked list, so the book can grow without a fixed size.
steps.done: you can add 10 contacts and print them all.
steps.hint: Add `struct contact *next;` to the struct. Adding at the front is the easiest: the new one points to the old first.
steps.why: Each element knows where the next one is. A linked list grows one piece at a time, and drawing it on paper (boxes and arrows) is the best way to get it right.

steps.do: Search for a contact by name.
steps.done: an existing name is found, and a missing one prints "not found".
steps.hint: Walk the list with `for (p = head; p; p = p->next)` and compare with `strcmp`.
steps.why: Comparing strings with `==` compares addresses, not text. `strcmp` compares the letters.

steps.do: Delete a contact from the list, and free its memory.
steps.done: the deleted contact no longer shows up, whether it was first, in the middle or last.
steps.hint: Keep a pointer to the previous element; the first element is a special case (or use a pointer to a pointer).
steps.why: Deleting from a list has edge cases: first, last, only one. Testing each is how you find the bug that only shows up sometimes.

steps.done: valgrind reports no leaks and no errors.
steps.hint: Compile with `-g`, run `valgrind --leak-check=full ./contacts`, and free the whole list before exiting.
steps.why: Leaks and invalid reads don't always crash; they wait. valgrind shows them now, with the line where they started.

steps.do: Save the contacts to a text file when the program ends, and load them when it starts.
steps.done: the contacts are still there after restarting the program.
steps.hint: One contact per line, fields separated by a character that can't be in a name (a tab, for example).
steps.why: Choosing a separator that can't appear in your data avoids a whole class of bugs. That's why CSV needs quotes and tabs are often simpler.

steps.do: Handle bad input: a too-long name, a broken line in the file, a missing file at the first start.
steps.done: none of them crashes the program.
steps.hint: `fgets` with the size of the buffer cuts long input; check what `sscanf` returns; a missing file just means an empty book.
steps.why: Defensive code expects the impossible. A missing file at the first start isn't an error, it's normal.

steps.do: Add a menu loop: add, list, search, delete, quit.
steps.done: you can do everything without restarting.
steps.hint: A `while` loop, a number or a letter read with `fgets`, and a `switch`.
steps.why: The menu ties all the functions together into a program someone else could use.

steps.do: Split the code into .c and .h files, and build it with a Makefile.
steps.done: `make` builds the program, and changing one file only rebuilds that one.
steps.hint: contact.h holds the struct and the function declarations; contact.c the code; main.c the menu.
steps.why: Real C projects are many files. A Makefile rebuilds only what changed, which matters when there are hundreds.

steps.do: Optional: sort the contacts by name, or export them as CSV.
steps.done: the list prints in alphabetical order.
steps.hint: Insert each new contact at the right place, or copy the pointers into an array and use `qsort`.
steps.why: Keeping a list sorted as you insert, or sorting it all at once: two strategies with different costs. Both are good to know.
